newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Southern African nations seek closer economic ties.
newsitem.headline: Southern African nations seek closer economic ties.

text.p: Southern African finance ministers on Friday said they were aiming to produce a draft agreement on economic policy convergence in the region by next April.

The blue print for closer economic cooperation among the 12-member Southern African Development Community (SADC) will be a first draft and ministers stressed it did not represent an aim for a European Union-style pact.
"We have not signed our equivalent of a Maastricht Treaty," said South African Finance Minister Trevor Manuel.
Ministers, who had just completed an annual meeting of SADC's finance and investment group, said they wanted to present a unified picture of Southern Africa to outside investors.

The best way to do this would be to converge economic policies, break down trade barriers and encourage multilateral projects such as the Gauteng-Maputo Corridor linking South Africa's most industrialised province with Mozambique's capital.
"We believe economic convergence has to happen...I think policy convergence is on the agenda," said Mauritian Finance Minister Rundheersing Bheenick.

One potential problem the region faces is the overwhelming dominance of South Africa in SADC. The country's huge industries and well developed financial sector have give it a big advantage in the group.
But ministers said South Africa should be an engine of growth for the whole region, winning itself new markets while giving the economies of its neighbours much-needed investment.
South Africa has also been plagued by a steady flood of illegal immigrants from nearby countries as its mines and industry attract the jobless from all over the continent.
Encouraging development beyond its own borders could help stem the flow. "South Africa has a vested interest in our prosperity," said Botswanan Vice-President and Finance Minister Festus Mogae.
But the region faces notable difficulties, especially as the recent collapse of the price of bullion may bite deep into South Africa's gold mining industry, triggering huge potential job losses.
Analysts say more than 50,000 miners, many of them from other SADC countries, could lose their jobs if the gold price falls below its current 12-year low.

The effects could ripple out and deal a blow to the regional economy. Lesotho Finance Minister Leketekete Ketso said 50 percent of his country's earnings came from migrant workers sending their wages back to the tiny, mountainous kingdom.
But he stressed Lesotho was mulling new labour-intensive schemes and the gold price could rise again and prevent mass lay-offs.
The problem highlights the desperate need for jobs in the region and labour-absorbing projects are going to be a key part of future cooperation.
But last year SADC members saw an average economic growth of 6.6 percent and several countries have battled inflation down into single digit figures.

South Africa's Manuel said SADC's economic prospects were fundamentally rosy. "A whole range of indicators are showing very positive trends...to many people SADC is going to be a motor force for economic transformation on the African continent," he said.
